definition: Mordant means bitingly witty — humor or criticism with a dry, cutting edge meant to leave a mark.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word mordant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know mordant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The playwright's mordant curtain speech thanked the critics 'for attending in shifts,' and the line drew laughter and blood in equal measure.
Wry is milder than mordant: a wry aside raises one eyebrow at the mess and means no harm, while mordant wit bites down hard enough to leave a mark.
Venomous goes further than mordant: mordant humor still wants the laugh it earns, but a venomous line has stopped joking and exists only to poison and wound.

Caustic criticism burns like the chemical it is named for — harsh, corrosive, and openly angry, with no obligation to amuse anyone. Mordant carries the same acid but delivers it as wit: the line entertains the room even as it bites its target.

A barbed remark is fitted with a hook — built to snag and sting on its way past. Mordant goes beyond the single barb: it is a whole manner of humor, dry and controlled, in which every joke carries its own point.

Mordant means bitingly witty — humor or criticism with a dry, cutting edge meant to leave a mark.

The staff cartoonist never raised her voice in the news meeting; she saved it for the page, where one mordant caption — the governor cutting a ribbon on a bridge to nowhere, labeled 'Progress' — did more damage than the editorial printed beside it.
Mordant is wit with teeth.
It is quieter than scathing (this unit): a scathing verdict batters its target openly, while a mordant line amuses the room and lets the target feel the sting a beat later.
And the sting is no accident — mordant humor is dry, deliberate, and precise, funny to everyone except the person bitten.
Mordant is the connoisseur's word for wit with teeth, and it is a scalpel rather than a bludgeon: dry, precise, never shouted.
Curt and brusque (this unit) are about giving too few words; mordant is about what a few well-chosen words can do.

Reserve it for humor, satire, and criticism — a mordant essay, a mordant aside — and note its day job: dyers and printers use mordant as a noun for the chemical that bites color into cloth, the same Latin teeth at honest work.

For his final broadcast, the station gave its retiring weatherman ninety seconds to say goodbye.

He used them to forecast the station's future: 'Cloudy, with a strong chance of reruns, and viewers advised to seek shelter from the nine o'clock lineup.' The control room laughed so hard the credits rolled late — and the program director's smile, colleagues noted, never reached his eyes.
Critics called the send-off mordant: every line got its laugh, and every laugh left a tooth mark somewhere in the building.
The station aired it too, having apparently decided that being bitten in public was better than being ignored.
